criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to municipal/public drinking water supply networks and household water security (quantity, quality, reliability, coping mechanisms, and accessibility) in Guwahati city, India.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails Criterion 2 under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, the study does not empirically examine any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, official discretion, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). While a brief subsection on illegal water connections notes a grievance cell, penalties, and lack of metering/field audits, that discussion is descriptive background drawing on media reports rather than an empirically analysed exposure. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2, although the paper invokes 'urban water governance', inadequate municipal funds, and provider management challenges as macro-background and tabulates public water schemes operated by different municipal/state bodies, its actual study design and empirical exposure examine physical water infrastructure (obsolete vs. newly commissioned plants, capacity gaps, pipe leakages/bursts) and spatial geography (distance and slope/elevation from service reservoirs across Zones I, II, and III), rather than a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical evidence from a structured household survey of 506 connected households across 25 water supply schemes conducted during 2022-2024, laboratory testing of tap-water samples (chlorine, turbidity, iron, pH, TDS, hardness, fluoride, calcium, magnesium), GIS mapping of water networks, and secondary data on treatment plant capacities and production.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple household water service access outcomes, including citywide public network access (34%), supply days per week, supply minutes per day, water quantity received (liters per supply and liters per capita per day, lpcd), tap-water quality across spatial zones, coping strategies for unreliability, and the percentage of households obtaining adequate water.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (506 connected households across 25 water supply schemes in Guwahati city, India), exposure (water infrastructure scheme characteristics and spatial distance/elevation from service reservoirs across Zones I, II, and III), outcomes (water quantity in lpcd, supply frequency/duration, water quality, coping strategies, and adequacy), and study design (cross-sectional household survey with laboratory water testing and GIS analysis) are clearly identifiable, though the exposure is physical/spatial infrastructure rather than an eligible legal or governance mechanism.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English (pages 1-14, with a Ukrainian summary on page 15).

study_design: Cross-sectional household questionnaire survey (purposive multi-zone spatial sampling across 25 water supply schemes), laboratory tap-water quality analysis, GIS mapping, and secondary institutional data assessment
population_and_sample: Households connected to urban public water supply systems in Guwahati city, Assam, India (506 surveyed households purposively sampled across 25 water supply schemes and 3 distance zones: 173 in Zone I, 165 in Zone II, and 168 in Zone III, alongside citywide secondary data on 135 water plants)
exposure: Prevailing physical urban water supply infrastructures (old vs. newly commissioned water treatment plants and deep tube well schemes, plant production capacity gaps, ageing pipes and leakages) and spatial location (distance and elevation/slope from service reservoirs across Zones I, II, and III)
outcome: Household water security dimensions: municipal water supply coverage (34% citywide), supply frequency (days/week and times/day), supply duration (minutes/day), water quantity (liters per supply and lpcd), tap-water quality (chlorine, turbidity, iron, TDS, pH, hardness, calcium, magnesium, fluoride), household coping mechanisms, and water accessibility (% of households obtaining adequate water)
rationale: This empirical geography study surveys 506 connected households across 25 urban water supply schemes in Guwahati, India, and tests tap-water samples to assess household water security (quantity, quality, reliability, coping strategies, and accessibility). Although it clearly examines household water service access (C1) with empirical household outcomes (C3, C4), its analysed exposures are physical infrastructure attributes (obsolete vs. newly commissioned plants, capacity gaps, pipe leakages/bursts) and spatial geography (distance and slope from service reservoirs across Zones I, II, and III). References to urban water governance, municipal funding shortages, and media-reported water theft/lack of metering serve only as unanalysed background context rather than an empirically studied legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance mechanism (failing C2 under both the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading and the plain reading). Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure).
